summary: On Mars, help from Earth is twenty minutes away, so a crew has to catch health risks before they happen. Most monitoring tools report how the body is doing right now; SpaceFuzz asks what today's plan will do to it. Every morning it builds a simple digital twin of the crew member from the check-in and stress-tests the day's schedule the way security engineers fuzz software: thousands of simulated what-if days (less sleep, a longer spacewalk, a CO2 excursion, a solar particle event) built from real NASA data on ISS cabin air and Mars-surface radiation. It finds where the body breaks first and the smallest change that would push it over the edge, then adjusts the plan and re-tests the fix before anyone acts on it. In our main scenario, a spacewalk after a short night carries a 21.0% risk; splitting and shortening the spacewalk and adding a nap brings it to 4.9%, without cutting tonight's sleep. A midday re-check and a crew visor HUD close the loop. The same idea, heat building up over a shift, fixed by changing the schedule, carries over to construction workers in hot, humid cities such as Singapore.
details:
What it does and how it works

SpaceFuzz forecasts the health risk of an astronaut's day and fixes the plan before the day begins.

  • Morning check-in: sleep over the last three nights, blood pressure, glucose, mood, stress, fatigue and an optional reaction test. A data-quality gate rejects implausible or missing values, so a forecast is never built on bad data.
  • Simulation: a body-state model, a simple digital twin of the crew member, steps through the day in 15-minute intervals, tracking heart rate, HRV, core temperature, SpO2 and fatigue. The environment is replayed from real data: ISS cabin CO2, temperature and humidity (NASA OSDR EDA) and Mars-surface radiation (NASA RadLab, MSL-RAD).
  • Fuzzing: six mutation operators perturb the day. Three map onto NASA's spaceflight hazards (solar particle events for radiation, sleep debt for isolation, cabin CO2 for the closed environment); the other three model workload and sensor faults. A probability track of 2,500 simulated days gives the risk, while a guided track of 10,000 rounds hunts for the ways the day can fail. A crash-boundary map shows the smallest change that breaks the plan.
  • Rules: eight deterministic health rules with sourced thresholds, such as NASA-STD-3001's 140 bpm line, where EVA performance starts to suffer, and a 6-hour sleep line from a study of 24 ISS astronauts.
  • Adjustment and re-test: candidate fixes (moving, shortening, or splitting the EVA, adding rest or a nap, postponing) are tried, smallest change first. A fix is accepted only if the risk stays at or below 5% and the plan survives a 30-minute schedule slip. Planned sleep is never cut. If no fix works, the plan is escalated to the ground flight surgeon.
  • Midday check: at 14:00, one value is remeasured, and only the rest of the day is reforecast and replanned.

Results

These results are built on open data. Most first-hand astronaut health data is held in NASA's Life Sciences Data Archive and requires a formal application, so the personal baseline here is synthetic. With more real astronaut data, the same engine would produce more accurate forecasts.

  • In our main scenario, a spacewalk after a short night carries a 21.0% risk, and just 15 minutes less sleep would raise it to 100%. The adjusted plan brings it down to 4.9%.
  • In the radiation scenario, a solar particle warning overlaps the planned spacewalk (100% risk); moving the spacewalk after the warning brings it to 3.0%. Starting right as the warning ends failed the re-test, so the plan keeps a 30-minute margin.
  • In the high-CO2 scenario, no fix gets below 32.3%, so the case goes to the ground.
  • At midday, a wristband reading of 5.9 h of sleep makes the afternoon spacewalk critical; moving it to 18:00 brings the risk back to 4.9% without cutting tonight's sleep.

Factors we considered

  • Creative thinking: we applied fuzz testing, a cyber-security technique, to a human's day. The plan is the program, the body is the system under test, and a "crash" is a broken health rule. Like a software patch, every fix is fuzzed again before it is recommended.
  • Evidence: real NASA data where available, and all 14 indicators checked one by one against NASA risk pages, NASA-STD-3001, and clinical guidelines.
  • Honesty about limits: thresholds and parameters are illustrative, so the results support the ranking of risks and the change before and after an adjustment, not absolute probabilities. Blood pressure and glucose are example values, the crew member is fictional, and gravity is not modelled.
  • Licensing: WESAD is licensed for non-commercial use only, so the repository holds just the fitted parameters.

Benefits and impact

  • Changes the question from "How am I now?" to "What will today's plan do to me?", early enough to act on the answer.
  • Delivers a clear result: one risk number, the system most at risk, the cause, a re-tested fix, and the one measurement to confirm first.
  • Matches the response to the risk (self-care, crew reminder or flight surgeon), supporting the flight surgeon rather than replacing them.
  • Runs offline and reproducibly, which matters when Earth is 20 minutes away.
  • Reaches beyond space: the same mechanism (heat building up over a shift) and the same fix (splitting long exposures and adding cooling breaks) can protect construction workers in hot, humid cities such as Singapore.

Tools

Python 3.11 with pandas, NumPy, SciPy, xarray, Streamlit, Plotly, Jupyter, Matplotlib, and Playwright; pytest and Hypothesis for about 870 tests; FFmpeg for the video. AI tools: Claude, Claude Code, and ElevenLabs (see Use of Super Intelligence).

It runs on a laptop: no GPU, no cloud, and no network needed at runtime.
